#3974. Heartopia celebrates 30 million downloads with new outfits, permanent price cuts

Heartopia's rise has continued since its launch earlier this year, and the game's developer isn't slowing down with updates.

Heartopia has kicked off a new event to celebrate passing 30 million downloads. Just a couple of weeks after delivering the vintage Hollywood-themed Dreamlight Cinematics event, developer XD Games has revealed The Whimsical Tea Party, a limited-time Gilded Acorn Exhibition.

The event kicked off on Saturday, bringing some new themed content to the game.

Whimsical Tea Party’s biggest addition are the new outfits, including the Wandering Traveler, and the Duke Bunny outfits. Each outfit is available in three different colours. Another thing Heartopia events bring are building materials sets.

This one adds the Labyrinth furniture building materials set, the Hedgehog & Flamingo mallet, and the Cheshire Cat pet costume. Speaking of outfits, XD Games is dropping the in-game prices for a number of items permanently.

All original pet outfits now cost 66.7% less. Those of the Common variety will now cost 10 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, instead of the previous 30. Rare pet outfits will cost 5 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, down from 15.

If you happened to buy Common or Rare original pet outfits between July 17, 2024 and March 22, 2026, you’ll be refunded the difference. This will automatically show up in-game the next time you log in. If you instead purchased those pet outfits between March 23 and April 4, you should look forward to your refund before April 10.

Keeping with the theme of freebies, Heartopia is also celebrating surpassing 30 million downloads worldwide by giving all players a small gift package in-game. This freebie is available until May 29, so you should have enough time to claim it.

For comprehensive guidance on where to find birds, bugs, and fish, check out our Heartopia bird locations, Heartopia bug locations, and Heartopia fish locations guides. If you’re instead looking to find some wild vegetables for those cooking recipes, hit those links. And, as ever, it doesn’t hurt to see if you missed out on any Heartopia codes.

#3973. SteamDB will add "affiliate links to authorised game retailers" and a new tab dedicated to mods, first update since Nexus Mods takeover confirms

"We're still in the early stages of what we want to achieve"

In a first substantial update since acquiring SteamDB from its founders back in September, the owners of Nexus Mods have outlined some new additions coming to , the two sides in the deal have announced some additions coming to the community-run backend database. Affiliate links aimed at providing options to help folks find the cheapest price for a game and a new tab dedicated to the mods Nexus host for a game are incoming, as work on behind-the-scenes improvements continues.

"We're now a couple of months in since [the takeover] announcement, so I thought it was about time we shared a quick update on what we've been working on behind the scenes, along with a few changes you'll start to see rolling out over the coming weeks," Victor Folmann, CEO of Nexus Mods owners Chosen wrote in a blog post on SteamDB.

There are two main new features he pointed to that you'll notice popping up on SteamDB soon. The first is one that anyone could have seen coming, a new tab on each moddable game's page that shows off some mods hosted for it on Nexus Mods and a host of modding-related data. "The new tab will help you discover mods for games you're browsing on SteamDB, making it easier to see whether a game has an active modding community and explore what it has to offer," Fomann wrote. "For now, we'll only be showing mods from Nexus Mods, as we already have access to that wealth of modding data, making it a straightforward starting point for this new feature.

"We appreciate that some of you might be wondering why we're not including Steam Workshop, too. It's certainly something we'd be open to exploring as we develop the feature further, along with other modding sources. With that in mind, if you run a modding website and would be interested in having your community's mods included, we'd love to hear from you."

That seems perfectly fine, but the other incoming feature's a bit more controversial given SteamDB's historically not been all about the money. "One thing we've seen people ask for is an easier way to find the cheapest place to buy a game, and we're now working on making that possible," Folmann wrote. "We'll be introducing affiliate links to authorised game retailers, giving you more options when looking for the best available price on a game.

"We recognise that introducing affiliate links may raise some concerns, so we want to be clear about how they'll work. First and foremost, as I mentioned, we'll only feature authorised retailers; we will not be including grey-market resellers. We've also made a deliberate decision about how prices are displayed: retailers will be ordered by the cheapest available price in your currency, not by whichever retailer offers us the highest affiliate commission. If a retailer doesn't offer pricing in your currency, we'll still show deals in other currencies provided they are available in your region."

Folmann was clear in the initial announcement of the takeover that Nexus Mods' bosses would be actively looking into ways SteamDB could make more money to sustain itself, so the addition of these links isn't out of the blue either. Whether SteamDB regulars agree that they're a "lighter-touch" way of earning the site some cash without detracting from the traditional experience of using it is another matter. I'll need to see how I feel once I've actually navigated a few pages with the links in as part of looking up stuff about games, but my first instinct is that as long as the pages don't end up revolving around the links and it's still easy to get to the info you want without interacting with them, I probably won't be too put out.

Beyond those tweaks, Folmann mentioned "improvements to how updates are tested before they go live" and how quickly the team can react to issues have been among the less obvious work going on behind the scenes. "We're still in the early stages of what we want to achieve, and there's plenty more work we need to do and would like to work on," he wrote in closing.

Folmann and co only took over Nexus Mods in June last year, making them still relatively new custodians of both it and SteamDB.

#3972. Final Fantasy Resonance Devs Surprised by How Many Fans Wanted a Traditional, Turn-Based RPG

Final Fantasy Resonance has been one of the most positively-received Square Enix games in ages — but its developers were never fully convinced that it would, er, resonate on the scale that it has.

Producer Keisuke Nakashima told Japanese outlet Game*Spark (as translated by Automaton): "I was surprised to see just how many people, not only in Japan but overseas as well, are eager for the kind of FF they remember from back in the day, with classic turn-based battles and pixel art."

Of course, this quote feeds into a debate that's been raging amongst fans of Final Fantasy for over a couple of decades at this point.

There are many who believe that the series has long since lost its way, pushing to innovate with more and more action-focused gameplay instead of drawing from the turn-based and command battle systems that helped establish the franchise as a world-beater in the first place.

Titles like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 are constantly brought up as living proof that turn-based RPGs can still be blockbusters — but Square Enix has only veered further and further away from Final Fantasy's traditional blueprint with each mainline instalment.

Resonance may be a lower-budget spin-off, but at least to some extent, it does go against the publisher's line of thinking that Final Fantasy must appeal to a "wider audience" if it's to maintain its flagship status.

"We figured [Resonance] was something we ourselves would enjoy, and that there would be players out there who’d feel the same way," says Nakashima.

Director Hiroto Furuya adds: "I thought this was a rather unconventional title, so I expected opinions on it might be divided."

He then references Resonance's foundations, having been built on the bones of now defunct mobile title Final Fantasy Brave Exvius: "I think the fact that a game with such an unusual background has been embraced by so many people is a positive for the industry as a whole, and I’m personally very happy to see it."

Without wanting to be overly critical of games I really enjoy, like Final Fantasy 16, I do think Square Enix has been guilty of chasing a goal that simply may not exist.

This mythical "wider audience" has been the downfall of many games over the years, and you can argue that Final Fantasy has chipped away at its own identity and strength of brand in the (pretty desperate) pursuit of new fans.

Resonance isn't going to sell millions upon millions of copies, but the way it's been embraced says a lot about the current state of Final Fantasy as a whole, I feel.

And remember, recent reports strongly suggested that the suits at Square Enix wanted Resonance to be a basic port of the aforementioned mobile title, presumably in a bid to keep costs down.

Are you glad Final Fantasy Resonance exists? Do you think Square Enix needs to learn from its success? Take a turn in the comments section below.

#3971. Honkai: Star Rail players are eating good, with Version 4.2 and third anniversary celebrations kicking off later this month

Honkai: Star Rail will be celebrating its third anniversary just days after it delivers a major update, and there's quite a bit to chew on in this one.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a stacked Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, delivering the one-two punch of revealing the game’s next major update, and detailing what you can expect from its third anniversary celebrations.

First off, Version 4.2, dubbed So Laughed the Masses, arrives April 22, making two characters playable, and bringing back a host of beloved characters for re-runs. The new update continues the Phantasmoon Games arc, as the story takes an especially suspect new development.

The big inciting incident of this new chapter is the reveal that whoever wins the Phantasmoon Games will also become the permanent Aeon of Elation. Meanwhile, Fulwish has invited all Supplicants to the Fulwish TV HQ to announce their intention to host a TV debate about the ultimate goal of the Phantasmoon Games.

Naturally, you’re invited, and you’ll have to overcome the challenges that await to gather more Wishpower.

Our first new arrival is Silver Wolf LV.999, with whom you should already be familiar from her Version 1 form. The difference now, of course, is that she’s getting a brand-new alternate kit, since — true to her new name — she's evolved into a Godmode Player upon reaching Level 999. Silver Wolf LV.999 is a 5-Star Imaginary character on the Path of Elation.

Her main combat trick is the ability to rack up Hidden MMR, which is what allows her to eventually activate her Cartridge and settle into the aforementioned Godmode state. While in that form, she shifts the entire battle into the virtual world, pulling in both teams into her gaming domain.

This is essentially a world under her control, which is why she can unlock a Reward Stage at the start of her turn, which lets her spawn in-game items. When picked up, these items can turn the tide of battle.

Keeping up with the ultra-gamer persona, Silver Wolf's Aha Instant strike blasts all enemies with a laser cannon, dealing massive damage. Perhaps her most interesting ability is being able to hack into the battlefield when she’s not actively on the team, something she can do when a teammate falls under enemy control.

Evanescia is the other newly-playable character, who has thus far only been an observer of the Phantasmoon Games, as well as one of the most prominent new characters we've met so far on Planarcadia. V4.2 sees the girl join the roster as a 5-Star Physical character who’s likewise on the Path of Elation. As she fights, she always accumulates Certified Banger, when she earns the title she’s able to simultaneously regenerate Energy and maintain her damage.

Evanescia’s damage continues to increase the more Certified Banger she accumulates, triggering an attack from Master Fox upon reaching a certain threshold, which deals damage to all enemies and regenerates Energy for herself. Her Elation Skill adds a bit of a performance to her kit, and is capable of hitting all enemies.

You may have noticed the Path of Elation theme in this one, so you won’t be surprised to learn that the Elation Trailblazer variant on the main playable character is also joining the team in 4.2. There’s a new weapon that starts off as a glow stick but can transform into a lightblade as you deal damage, and, yes, gain Certified Banger.

It can also turn into nunchucks, which delivers a unique flurry of attacks on all enemies surrounding the character, dealing multiple instances of damage. You can also use it to cheer for a teammate, hyping them up.

Version 4.2 Warp Events will bring back six characters. The first half will see reruns of The Dahlia, Castorice, and Firefly. The second half will give you another shot at unlocking Tribbie, Sunday, and Feixiao. What’s more, four of the game’s characters will be buffed in this update, so you may want to reconsider putting them them back on your team. They are Firefly, Huohuo, Seele, and Welt.

As part of the same update, you can expect the debut of the Cosmic Data Roaming event, which goes live alongside the anniversary celebrations. The event lets you live the life of a streamer.

Currency Wars is getting a big expansion, too. Likewise, the Cosmicon Collective is getting its version 2.0 update, adding new decks, dice as well as a new team challenge game mode.

As for the big third anniversary celebration, it will kick off in-game on April 26, bringing back Festive Gifts. The event will only be available during these celebrations, and it will once again be gifting players who log in regularly a total of 20 pulls.

You’ll also be able to a select a blessing card from a companion of your choice to receive a special gift of 1,600 Stellar Jades. The same celebrations will also seeHuohuo and Robin permanently added to the Stellar Convergence store. You’ll have another chance to exchange a Golden Companion Spirit for any companion you like in that store, too — and all you need to do is log in anytime between Versions 4.2 and 4.4. This being a new year for Honkai: Star Rail, the top-up double bonus is resetting, meaning anyone who tops up their wallet will get a hefty bonus.

Elsewhere, you’ll find new items in the Gift of Stardust Store, including a new outfit for Castorice. Between the time 4.2 launches and when the celebrations begin, you’ll be able to try your luck in Aha's Chosen: Spreading Elation Everywhere, an online event where you can leave a message for a chance to win various prizes.

#3970. GTA 6 Appears To Be Causing Issues On A Small Number Of Xbox (& PS5) Consoles

FWIW, it seems to be happening more on PS5

Over the last few days, I've been running into various bits of discussion on social media about how GTA 6 is crashing or even "frying" some people's consoles, and for the most part it's been talked about in regards to the PS5 version.

This particular clip has been getting a ton of attention this week (profanity warning):

The Verge editor Tom Warren ended up picking up on this, suggesting that "GTA 6 is really stress testing the GPUs inside consoles", and then pointing out that the Xbox Support Reddit community highlights issues on Xbox as well.

And after visiting it, yeah... there's no doubt it's got multiple reports from people who claim GTA 6 has been responsible for either crashing their console or putting stress on the GPU and causing the visuals to stop functioning properly.

Here are just a few examples of people confirming their issues:

Now, as scary as this might seem, it's worth keeping in mind that you're unlikely to run into any major issues. The majority of GTA 6 players are enjoying the game just fine on their Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S and PS5 consoles right now, and I'm willing to bet most people haven't had a single crash whatsoever.

It also should be noted that Rockstar aimed to reduce crashes in their latest update for GTA 6 this week.

News GTA 6 Update Now Live On Xbox Series X|S, Includes Seven Official Fixes

Update: We've got the deets from Rockstar

At the same time, it's also impossible to say how widespread the problem is, but most people speculate that it's limited to anywhere between 0.1% and 5% of Xbox players at most. GTA 6 is an incredibly demanding game without a doubt, and it might unfortunately be exposing some weaknesses in certain consoles for whatever reason.

That's why we're only saying "a small number of" consoles in the headline here, because we don't want you to get scared off from playing GTA 6 over the next few weeks and months. Just keep in mind that it's a good idea to ensure your console isn't too clogged up with dust every now and again, and hopefully you'll never run into issues like this.

#3969. "It’s hard not to worry": Even as GTA 6 launches on console amid glowing reviews, Rockstar devs are already concerned about getting laid off

Even though they've "had no indication that layoffs are coming" from bosses

GTA 6 launches on console today. It's widely expected to sell more copies than main character Lucia Caminos has skin pores, more copies than there are words even in Eurogamer's five-star review, which I believe Chris Tapsell has written specifically to exhaust and destroy such neurones as I have remaining. And yet, staff at Rockstar Games are apparently worrying about being laid off, as development winds down and investors start to bicker about Line Going Up Even More.

In an article supporting this month's union vote at Rockstar North, one of the game's animation programmers argues that "workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

The animation programmer in question is Nestor Uriarte, writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section. Following some personal reflections on his time at the studio, he calls on other Rockstar devs to get behind the union, describing it as both "a huge step forward" for a company that has previously faced allegations of "crunch culture", and a win for UK game developers at large. "What happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more," Uriarte writes.

The vote at Rockstar North will run till 26th November, and could give rise to a union spanning over 1600 developers, according to umbrella organisation the Independent Workers of Great Britain. If that comes to pass, it would make the Rockstar union the largest recognised videogame developer union in the UK.

It comes as the company and a group of fired workers await the result of an employment tribunal battle over alleged "union-busting". Rockstar has accused the workers in question of "gross misconduct" and a breach of confidentiality by means of a union Discord server. Amongst other things, the legal brawl has revealed that Rockstar had a mole on that server for two and a half years, prior to the firings.

As for the prospect of further job losses, after GTA 6 goes on sale, Uriarte cites a wave of mass layoffs across the industry that has affected the creators of even commercially successful games like Battlefield 6 and Netflix's FIFA World Cup.

"After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds," he writes. "Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

The obvious context here is that GTA 6 has been a massively expensive production, with a development team headcount in the thousands. While one could accuse Uriarte of fear-mongering, I do find it hard to believe that executives at parent company Take-Two aren't weighing up some timely "down-sizing" right now. In general, videogame companies have a long tradition of axing the books once a game has been shipped, despite arguments that keeping experienced teams intact often pays off. In Rockstar's case, however, it's also worth bearing in mind that the GTA 6 rolling out this week is only part of the package. There's also the hazy prospect of the next incarnation of GTA Online, which – going by GTA 5 sales – will be a money spinner for many years, and will require a sizeable staff to maintain. Oh, and of course there's the PC version.

Echoing many peers, Uriarte also argues in his piece that it's important to unionise now in order to negotiate proper protection against generative AI cost-cutting initiatives. "The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry," he continues. "Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.

"Rockstar has said it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people," Urirarte concedes. "But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together."

The latest Japanese charts are in from Famitsu, and in perhaps the least surprising debut in recent memory, Grand Theft Auto VI is a hit.

Rockstar's code-in-a-box release had a staggering debut week in Japan, pulling in over 200,000 physical sales and kicking Ocarina of Time's comparatively measly ~35,000 into second. It's shy of the 537,000 Link's latest put up in its debut week, of course, but for a box with no disc in it, it's not bad going.

The rest of the chart is a Switch-fest, mind you, with the likes of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and Rhythm Heaven Groove still performing well, and last week's silver medallist, Metaphor: ReFantazio, hanging in there at ninth.

All of that GTA love means that Switch 2 has been dethroned as champion of the hardware charts this week. The PS5 Digital Edition sneaks into the top spot, with a perfectly respectable 40,362 sales to its name, while Nintendo's latest follows behind with ~36,000 of its own.

You don't need us to spell it out for you, but that means the PS5 wins the SKU race over the Switch 1 this week. Sony's three systems put up 41,472 total sales, while the Switch, Lite, and OLED combined for 4,362.

#3967. Animal Crossing: New Horizons gets a new item to celebrate 25 years of the series

The allegedly finished game might finally, truly be feature complete with the addition of an anniversary item.

Animal Crossing: New Horizons has received a surprise patch today to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the life sim series. The update, version 3.0.2, is available across the Switch and Switch 2 versions of the game.

The patch brings a single new addition to New Horizons - a leaf item. Everyone gets it, too, so you don’t have to do anything special to acquire it.

After installing the patch, simply head to your in-house mailbox to claim it. The mail includes a hearty message to fans who supported the series for years, featuring an appropriate Nintendo N64 stamp.

The Leaf Statue, as it’s referred to in-game, lights up when placed.

April 14, 2011 marks the release of the original, lesser-known version of Animal Crossing in Japan. The game was initially released as Animal Forest (Dobutsu no Mori) on the Nintendo N64, before later making its way to the Nintendo GameCube in December of the same year as Dobutsu no Mori+ with some extra features.

That same, original design of the package is also available for display in your game. The rest of the patch notes are entirely about various bug fixes, so not much more there. You can see the full change log on Nintendo’s support website.

#3966. I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish

At this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed. A familiar litany of unrealised ambition, heinous bugs, dull open-world design, and an expensive yet audibly bored voice cast, the accidental comedic highlight of which is Michelle Rodriguez flatly reeling off car theft orders from what sounds like the inside of a Michelle Rodriguez-sized tupperware container.

A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite. The 2003-2004 hype cycle had sowed the notion that this would in fact be the open-world crime thriller to knock Grand Theft Auto off its perch, and even 22 years before GTA 6's idolising reviews, that was no small promise; Rockstar were still enjoying the balmy success of Vice City, and we could see San Andreas cresting the hill on a stolen, shining BMX. "Ah, but did they have Michael Madsen doing doughnuts in car parks?," publishers Atari asked the world, either unaware or in denial of the spluttering, clapped-out rattletrap they were about to wheel into the showroom.

You likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance. I succumbed to this myself, having recently installed a legally unlinkable copy of Drivethreeuh, mind opened to the possibility that maybe it wasn't that bad. Six hours later, I am here to tell you: it was.

Almost nothing here works, figuratively and literally. Within three minutes of the opening mission, before Madsen's undercover cop Tanner goes undercover, you're ordered to join some marked police cars to head for a bust – but because the rozzers' primary function is to give chase to you, later on, driving too close crosses their wires, provoking them into blue-on-blue ramming maneuvres. Later, in a motorbike sprint down an inexplicably exploding beach, cartel goons are positioned across the sand, presumably to take drama-enhancing pot shots. They're so slow, however, both to notice your presence and to physically raise their guns, that they're barely out of their idle animations by the time you whizz past. And your own guy isn't much better: an assassination mission, which ends with your target cornered from an elevated position, requires that you take a few steps backwards first, as Tanner can't drop his shootin' arms low enough to land a hit from the balcony he's on.

Unlike Vice City's Tommy Vercetti, he can at least swim, which by 2004 standards gives the seaside Miami and Nice maps a fair verisimilitude, particularly when a shot-up boat engine forces the abandoning of ship. No amount of product-of-its-time concessions, though, can account for how woodenly unpalatable the on-foot action is. Controls are stiff and shooting feels meaningless, with zero tangible sense of bullets being sent nor received; killing a man carries all the weight of just shouting at him to lie down, and if it weren't for sound effects and the dwindling health bar, I could park Tanner in front of a firing squad of identically-modelled thugs with almost zero impression that his lungs were filling with Uzi rounds.

Driver, of course, began as a pure wheelman sim, later installments only letting you hoof it after someone at developers Reflections began smelling that Rockstar money. It was therefore always unlikely, even for the purported GTA killer, that this would achieve action-adventure sophistication in its bipedal bits. Even so, god, it's woeful. Stingy checkpointing also means that failure is often punished by having to replay those tedious, flavourless shootouts in full.

The driving is better, which is a bit like saying there's decent cheese in this cheese and smallpox toastie. It's reasonably slidey, when throwing the back end through a curving French alleyway, and in contrast to the gunplay, there is a somewhat realised tactility to ploughing around in two tonnes of rolling metal. It has problems of its own, mind. Cars feel okay when they're moving, but contact and crashes are leaden, sluggish, visually underwhelming occasions that I would call non-events, were they not so slow to recover from that a single nasty impact can scupper a timed mission. Granted, I quickly re-learned how vital it is to keep both eyes on the road, as other vehicles, pedestrians, lamposts, and other detritus tend to pop into existence some mere fifty feet in front of my speeding bumper.

The result, of both this graphical shortcoming and the overly punishing crashes, is a getaway car sim that too often encourages you to drive like cataract-ridden grandparent. Worse, whoever put Letty Ortiz in a lunchbox must have also been in charge of the engine noises, producing an array of miserable high-rev dins – especially for the motorbikes, which screech like amateurishly autotuned vacuum cleaners. There are also shades of that deranged cop AI in ordinary commuters, who I've repeatedly seen swerving and slaloming around empty lanes, seemingly for no reason beyond violent confusion.

Strangely enough, my 2026 return has largely dodged the game's infamous glitchiness, the worst instance of physics defiance being a garage door that appeared to lift Tanner into the air before propelling him, incorporeally, through the car shed's roof. I recall much worse, from the days when I'd have my dad rent it for me from Blockbuster. Mission-critical NPCs getting stuck on walls; flipped pursuit cars spinning endlessly; getting flung into space when walking on an overturned vehicle (a common occurrence, given the actual 'crawling out' animation sometimes failed to play, the game instead teleporting you onto the spring-loaded underside instead).

I've thus far escaped these, but as far as I know, they're still lurking dormant, and none of what I've witnessed with adult eyes has been funny or stupid enough to imbue Driv3r 3 The Third with a Wiseauean so-bad-it's-good quality. It's just bad. It was always bad. Why did I even entertain the possibility that it wasn't bad?

Reflections, to their credit, accepted their folly. Narratively unrelated sequel Driver: Parallel Lines tucked away a bin full of discarded copies, at least until Ubisoft bought up the series and patched it out, and for all the fantastical coma silliness of direct followup Driver: San Francisco, that was sensible enough to keep Tanner where he best belongs: hands on the wheel, foot on the gas, gun holstered. And was a far, far better game for it, too.

As 2011's San Francisco launch also remains the most recent Driver release, I regretfully can't end with the assurance that DrIIIver's legacy is a mere blip on a redeemed franchise. That stain stank, and did for ages, very possibly to the extent that GTA's one-time biggest rival never recovered.

Still, even if Reflections couldn't fully turn around their fortunes, the consistent improvement from this to Parallel Lines to San Francisco showed that they did learn something. Maybe so too did anyone else who went on to make an open-world action game. Which wouldn't be the worst outcome; after all, those who do not learn from gnarled, stinking wrecks like this are doomed to repeat them.

#3965. PS Plus Essential Games for December 2026 Announced

These games will be available to claim until 4th January, 2027 after they’ve been added to the sub next week.

It’s the final update of 2026 and PS Plus Essential is going out with a bit of a bang in my opinion.

Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3 + 4 is the most recent remake in Activision’s long-running skateboarding series, and a very good compilation at that.

We awarded it an 8/10 in our review, writing: “Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 + 4 is another fantastic skateboarding title that revives some all-time classics, albeit with some caveats.”

Meanwhile, Dragon Ball XenoVerse 2 is arriving just ahead of its sequel next year. This game has received years of support, including a fairly recent PS5 port, included here as part of your subscription.

Of that PS5 version, we wrote in our 7/10 review: “The only problem with XenoVerse 2, here in 2024, is that its core gameplay has never truly evolved. Yes, more and more ways to upgrade and customise your character have been added over the years, but the actual combat feels basic and a touch too finicky by today's standards.”

Finally, Amnesia: The Bunker is an acclaimed horror game from specialists Frictional – and one we ultimately liked.

We said in our 7/10 review: “Amnesia: The Bunker sticks a little too close to what Frictional Games has been doing for over a decade now, but with a more free-form approach to gameplay, the team is back on the right track again.”

That rounds out the lineup for December, then – and 2026 as a whole? How are you feeling about PS Plus Essential this year? Let me know below.

#3963. Metro 2039 goes back to its Metro underground roots, with a story shaped by the war in Ukraine and the people who suffer it

Metro 2039 takes us back to the tunnels of the Moscow Metro where, fittingly, Nazi ideology never died.

The Metro series is finally, officially back with a new installment. 4A Games has just unveiled Metro 2039 to the world, the follow-up to the outstanding Metro Exodus, released all the way back in 2019.

2039 takes an unusual route with its scope, however. Rather than build on the semi-open-world structure of Exodus, the upcoming sequel instead brings the focus back to where it all began: the Metro.

What won’t be changing is the kind of game that it is. Metro 2039 remains, like its predecessors, a story-driven, single-player game. Returning to the confined spaces of the Moscow Metro brings the focus back to the claustrophobic, uneasy atmosphere of the original games.

The game’s protagonist is, for the first time, going to be voiced throughout. From what we’ve been able to see, the psychological horror in this installment will be driven more by the very real effects the apocalypse has had, and continues to have, on denizens of the Metro.

2039 has been in development for years, but 4A Games has been rocked by two considerable events: the 2020 Covid pandemic, and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, where the developer is based. The game’s darker story has changed in response to that.

The team’s Ukrainian perspective is molded into the narrative, and more prominently represents the toll the events of the last several years has taken on members of the team, their families and communities.

According to the developer, you can expect a bigger emphasis on choice and consequence, with Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky returning to co-write a narrative that explores the compromised morality of a post-war society.

The new protagonist’s return to the Metro comes with the reveal that the different underground factions are now united under one banner, the not-so-subtly named Novoreich. Lead by a former Spartan, the Novoreich is an authoritarian regime which offers what it believes to be the only path to salvation.

4A Games remains majority Ukrainian, with teams based in Kyiv, and Malta. Unlike most AAA projects today, the studio continues to rely on its own engine tech. The 4A Engine is given a major upgrade for 2039: ray tracing is now a core component of the rendering pipeline, but the tech has been rebuilt to run better on modern hardware.

Today’s reveal sadly didn’t feature much gameplay - only a brief first-look with a mix of gameplay and cinematics. The developer, however, emphasised that creating cluttered, believable and lived-in environments remains a key focus.

Metro 2039 is set for release sometime this winter on PC, Xbox Series X/S, and PS5.

#3962. Blizzard will talk about Diablo 4: Lord of Hatred one last time before the expansion's launch next week

We're well under two weeks from the launch of Diablo 4's next expansion, Lord of Hatred, but there's more yet to be said.

Diablo 4 is mere days away from the launch of its biggest expansion yet, and Blizzard wants to make sure it got one last chance to tell you about it. Lord of Hatred is the follow-up to 2024’s Vessel of Hatred, and it’s set to arrive on April 28.

Next week, however, we’re getting an updated look at the new content as part of a livestream. This is the Developer Update kind; the meaty, information-dense show anyone who follows Diablo’s livestreams should be familiar with.

The next Developer Update is set for Thursday, April 23. It’ll kick off at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 6pm GMT. The show will, naturally, focus on Lord of Hatred. In particular, we’re getting another look at the expansion content that hasn’t been given the same level of coverage as the bigger features.

Everyone knows about the new Skovos region, the Warlock class (and the Paladin before that), but we haven’t seen much from the other gameplay-altering features that affect a lot of the core flow.

In next week’s showcase, Blizzard will show off the updated and expanded skill trees - which come to all classes, the Talisman system, and the gear-altering Horadric Cube. War Plans, the new make-your-own-endgame feature will be discussed, too.

More interestingly, we’re also going to hear about the new season kicking off right alongside the launch of Lord of Hatred. A short, in-betweener season is currently live in Diablo 4, and it’s going to end right as the next one/the expansion launch.

And, of course, the show won’t end before the team takes a few questions from chat, as is tradition. If you want to catch it live, you’ll be able to do so on Diablo’s official YouTube, Twitch, Twitter, and TikTok channels.

#3961. "Abducting your own lover no longer gives you opinion of yourself" declare the notes for Crusader Kings 3's free Florin update, released alongside Silk and Silver

Funky feudal family frolic Crusader Kings 3 got its second major expansion of the year this week. It's called Silk and Silver (read my impressions), is all about merchant republics, and shipped alongside a beefy free update to the base game which - while largely focused on overhauling economics - also has some funny patch notes and features worth being aware of.

The main features of the free 'Florin' update are outlined by Paradox in the video above, and unless you're really into the nitty gritty details of realm and wealth management, there's one bit of it which stands out. The option to play as a landless adventurer has finally made its way into the base game, as Paradox promised earlier this year.

This means you can kick off a playthrough as a lowborn leader of a travelling band or a wandering noble with claims on realms ruled by others. Originally locked behind the Roads to Power DLC, the option to start off this way or end up living if you end up deposed from your throne of choice is a great addition to the story arc of any CK3 run. No longer are you glued to the throne from day one to the day you quit for good - power's a privilege which can be earned and revoked depending on what you get up to. Though, it's worth noting that only three ways of operating as a landless adventurer are being made free to access with this update. You can be an aimless wanderers, sword-toting mercenaries, or scholars. If you want your band to earn their living as explorers, free booters, or legitimists, you'll still need Roads to Power.

As for the rest of the free additions, community manager Jacob Blakey summed them up thusly:

#3960. Xbox Fans Make Their Feelings Known In Response To Yooka-Laylee Upgrade Announcement

The new Definitive Edition appears to skipping the platform

Here's a strange one for you! The fantastic Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair has been one of the best platformers on Xbox since it launched back in 2019, but the game's new "Definitive Edition" appears to be skipping Series X and S.

A new announcement today revealed that the upgraded Definitive Edition will include enhanced visuals, up to 4K resolution at 120FPS, two orchestrated soundtracks and more, but it will only be available on PC, Switch 2 and PS5.

As you can imagine, that hasn't gone down well with Xbox fans.

The comments section of Playtonic Games' post is full of reactions like these, and at the time of writing, no response or statement has been provided for why the Definitive Edition isn't coming to Xbox in addition to other platforms.

There may well be a very good reason for it, and here's hoping we might get clarification at some point in the near future, but at least for the time being, it seems we're going to have to miss out on this new enhanced version.

As disappointing as this is, the 2019 original is still well worth playing if you're interested!

#3959. Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair Gets a PS5 Definitive Edition, Out This December

Playtonic has announced Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair is being treated to a new Definitive Edition on PS5, and it's right around the corner.

The new version launches on 15th December 2026, and anyone who owns a digital PS4 version of the game gets a free upgrade. It appears anyone with a physical copy won't get the upgrade.

On base PS5 and PS5 Pro, the new edition will support a 4K resolution at 120fps, better lighting and ambient occlusion effects, higher-fidelity shadows, and two orchestrated soundtracks. Also, if you don't already own it, the Trowzer's Top Tonic Pack is automatically bundled in with the PS5 version.

One of the best platforming adventures of its generation is back, enhanced for PlayStation 5. Yooka & Laylee return for a full-scale 2.5D adventure, with a 3D Overworld that's an adventure in its own right, levels you can alter to create new ways to play, and Capital B's Impossible Lair waiting to test your skills.

A 2D and top-down side game that accompanies the main Yooka-Laylee game, the Impossible Lair went down really well upon its original launch. It's got an 82 rating on Metacritic, and in our own review, we called it an "improvement" on the original adventure.

Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.

#3958. The Sims 4's much maligned paid mods have made it to consoles, but Kits are coming back to PC

The Sims 4's Marketplace and user-created content have officially arrived on consoles, a little over a month after their debut on PC.

The Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace. This new feature is essentially a hub for paid mods and other user-created content.

As often happens when long-established games introduce paid mods, The Sims 4’s wasn’t especially well-received, in part because of the introduction of a new premium currency - Moola - that is the only way to purchase any of that content.

The Moola denominations and prices are similar to many other in-game currencies, and the criticism around them is the same: they obfuscate the true value of items, and because of the way those denominations are structured, you’ll never be able to buy exactly what you need.

For most games, the subject of paid mods has always been fraught, and that's certainly true for The Sims 4. In the announcement blog post, Maxis said that the launch on consoles will work similarly to what PC players have seen, in that Kits will no longer be available to buy directly with real money on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores. While Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs will remain, you’ll need to buy Moola if you want to acquire Kits going forward.

Interestingly, however, EA seems to have changed its mind somewhat on the Kits situation. A recently leaked memo (via SimsCommunity), appears to show that the publisher intends on making Kits available for purchase directly again, without the need for Moola.

Unfortunately, this only appears to affect the PC version, with the reversion reportedly forthcoming on both the EA App as well as Steam. Indeed, according to the same report, the change has already taken place on the former, with the latter following on April 20.

Considering the Marketplace only just launched on consoles, the company may wait to see if the decision to remove Kits from console platform marketplaces will be as poorly received as it has been on PC.

If you’re looking to jump back into The Sims 4 to check out all the new paid content, make sure you’re well-equipped with our list of Sims 4 cheats and debug options, or this one specifically for the Royalty & Legacy expansion cheats.

#3957. Korridor turns those Youtube ads for vertical mobile shooters into a new, "deeply strategic" genre, and I can't decide if it's lying

The electro-metal OST seems legit, at least

I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

In Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

#3955. Review: Gamesir Nova Vision Controller For Switch 1 & 2 - Unique Features Elevate This Mid-Range Pad

Accessory developer Gamesir doesn’t often make controllers with the Switch 1 and 2 in mind, instead focusing primarily on Xbox and PC. So when it announced the new Nova Vision, my Spider-Sense tingled.

The latest entry in the mid-range Nova line, the Vision adds two unique features: a colour LCD screen for quick and easy customisation, and Hall Effect analogue sticks with adjustable tension without the need for extra tools. At $54.99, this is a compelling controller as it is, but Gamesir has also included a charging stand to ensure you’re always good to go.

The analogue sticks really are the star of the show. Featuring raised, textured edges with a grippy rubber material, they actually share much in common with the PS5 analogue sticks and feel great to use. The Hall Effect technology should keep stick drift at bay, while the transparent domes let you see into the interior – a neat little touch I personally liked. My wife wasn’t keen on it, so your own appreciation may vary.

Adjustable tension isn’t completely new — Gulikit’s TT Pro and Max controllers do the same thing — but this is the first instance I’ve tried a controller that lets you do it without any extra tools. All you need to do is twist the sticks anti-clockwise to loosen the tension, and clockwise to tighten.

At their loosest, the sticks feel light and floaty, good for open-world games like Breath of the Wild in which you need to move great distances. At their tightest, they allow for more precise movements, which might come in handy for racing games like Mario Kart World or first-person shooters like Modern Warfare 4.

Had it required an extra tool to adjust the tension, I might have just left the Nova Vision at one setting and been done with it. However, being able to simply twist the sticks to my desired tension at any point encouraged experimentation based on the game I’m playing. It’s a neat feature, and thankfully they take a fair bit of pressure to twist, so you’re never going to do it accidentally.

The screen acts as your main hub for functions and customisation. You might notice at first glance that the Vision is lacking buttons for Start, Select, and Home - they’re all housed in the screen. Click it on the bottom right for Start, the bottom left for Select, and anywhere near the top for Home.

Then you’ve got the ‘M’ button at the bottom, nestled in between the D-pad and right analogue stick. Hold this down for about five seconds to access the configuration menu. Here, you can select whether to connect to Switch, PC, or mobile, remap buttons to your liking, switch between profiles, adjust motion controls and vibration intensity, and more.

When you’re in the configuration menu, navigation is simple: use the D-pad to highlight menu items, ‘A’ to select, and ‘B’ to go back. When you’re done, just hold down the ‘M’ button again to exit. If you’re wondering where the capture button is, there isn’t one, but a quick double-tap of ‘M’ provides the same functionality. There’s no ‘C’ button for chat, mind you.

Inputs feel pretty good, overall. The D-pad, shoulder buttons, and back buttons are mechanical and provide a nice, satisfying click when pressed. The ABXY inputs, meanwhile, are membrane and considerably quieter by comparison. The main shoulder triggers can be swapped between full motion travel and short, clicky stops, so experiment with this to find your preference.

The back buttons aren’t mapped to anything by default. You can map any individual input to the buttons, or opt for any combo macro up to 12 inputs. They’re positioned nicely, allowing your middle fingers to rest comfortably, and they’re much quieter than some of the competition on the market.

Connection is done in three ways: Bluetooth, 2.4G wireless via a dongle, or a USB-C cable. The 1000mAh battery should comfortably last over 10 hours on a single charge, but if you’re using the included charging dock, you’ll likely never need to worry about this. The dock itself is pretty small and minimal in its design, with a nice, subtle RGB strip that slowly pulses when the controller is docked. And yes, it does feature wake-up support for Switch 2.

Finally, it’s worth mentioning that you can further customise the controller via the Gamesir Connect PC app, allowing you to add your own images and GIFs to the built-in screen. Unfortunately, the downside here is that it’s not compatible with Mac, so I’ve been unable to test this feature out myself.

For the mid-range price, the Nova Vision is an excellent controller for Switch 1 and 2. The built-in screen allows for quick customisation and remapping if needed, while the adjustable tension in the analogue sticks feels intuitive and genuinely useful for different games and genres. Add in Hall Effect technology and the charging dock, and you’re getting a lot of bang for your buck.

The lack of a ‘C’ button is a shame, while introducing Mac compatibility for the Gamesir Connect app would be an easy win. Furthermore, some folks just might not be keen on functions like Start and Home being accessed via the screen. If that’s you, then this probably isn’t for you. For everyone else, the Nova Vision is a solid choice.

#3954. Naval warfare, an actual server browser and more on the way to Battlefield 6 this year as BF Studios reveals 2026 roadmap

2026 is looking very exciting for Battlefield 6, even if much of what's coming is based on things we already know, and some we've long been asking for.

It took Battlefield Studios over four months to tell Battlefield 6 players what they can actually expect from the game over the course of this year, in terms of content - but we’re glad to see a plan laid out nonetheless.

The developer unveiled a grand 2026 roadmap, covering three more seasons currently in the works, and a wealth of new additions across the entire game, including new maps and the introduction of a new theatre of combat.

In a wide-ranging new video dubbed The Year Ahead, members of the Battlefield 6 development team have revealed a lot of new information about the future of the multiplayer shooter, going over plenty of the features and new content coming over the course of this year.

The video confirmed that BF6 has at least three other seasons in the works. Season 3, which begins in May, will be followed by Season 4, and Season 5 later in the year. Season 5 is the most mysterious, which is understandable.

We’ve known about some of what’s coming in Season 3, such as the remake of Golmud Railway (now called Railway to Golmud), but the video also revealed that a remake of Battlefield 3’s Grand Bazaar - now Cairo Bazaar - will also arrive later in the same season. Other exciting additions, such as battle royale solos and ranked play for Redsec are also on the agenda for Season 3.

Season 4, set for July, looks to be the biggest so far, with the introduction of naval combat, which will be available across two maps. Tsuru Reef, which is said to be even larger than Golmud, the largest map in BF6. The Pacific-set map won’t be the only one, as later in the season, another remake will arrive, this time of the iconic Wake Island.

The introduction of naval combat will bring with it a new dynamic wave system, aircraft carriers with operational flight decks, and new naval vehicles. Custom lobbies and Spectator Mode are also planned for Season 4.

Season 5 will bring three maps to BF6, rather than two, but all of its content remains under wraps.

Perhaps a sour note is that almost all of the maps referenced and shown in the video are remakes of maps from other Battlefield games, or reimagined at the very least. The Battlefield series is no stranger to remaking its own maps, but Battlefield 6 appears to be leaning on it much more than past entries.

If it’s any consolation, however, the map remakes we’ve played so far in Battlefield 6 have gone through major changes that have contributed to giving them a different flow and feel from their classic versions, or even remakes in other BF games.

Over the course of 2026, you can also expect the return of persistent servers, as well as a server browser to find them all - just like the good ol’ days. This includes the ability to host your own, though it’s unclear quite how this is going to work.

Season 3 is set to revealed in the coming days, so you’ll be hearing back from BF Studios in the near future.

#3953. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

#3952. 10+ Xbox Games Are Releasing Today, Including A Dangerous Twist On Mario Party (November 26)

"New twists on the party genre for sessions of fun, screaming, and horror"

December is just around the corner, yet we've still got plenty of November games to get through.

Also launching today is Security 51, another XPA title that's giving all sorts of Papers, Please vibes. Not everything is as it seems though, so keep your eyes peeled, yeah?

And finally, there's The Spectrum Retreat: Redux, a first-person puzzler from an award-winning game dev. Personally, I don't know much about this one, but on the surface, it looks pretty cool.

#3951. Diablo 4's next season won't have any new mechanics or a new theme because all the focus is on Lord of Hatred

If you don't intend to buy the Lord of Hatred expansion, the next season in Diablo 4 won't be as exciting as you'd expect.

Diablo 4 is gearing up for its biggest post-launch event yet: the upcoming release of the Lord of Hatred expansion. As was the case with Vessel of Hatred before it, expansion releases alter the seasonal flow in a few ways, and Blizzard has now explained how.

The game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning. The new season will kick off alongside the expansion’s release next week, and will be available to all players, just like all previous seasons.

Although Season of Reckoning will roll out as normal, the season itself won’t be as meaty, at least when it comes to the sort of gameplay mechanics and themes players have come to expect from each new season.

You’ll still find the normal Season Rank chase, Smoldering Ashes, and various rewards at each chapter. Season Blessings will also return, but that’s about it for progression outside of the game itself. If it’s any consolation, there are more goals and objectives to tackle this season.

The even better news is that, according to Blizzard, future seasons will follow the classic format, which makes sense. The new season will come with a battle pass, of course, featuring four Reliquaries, as usual. The first Reliquary is free, while the others are paid.

Blizzard has also confirmed the the pre-load for Lord of Hatred is available now on all platforms. Even if you’re not getting the expansion, patch 3.0.0's pre-load includes all expansion content regardless, so you may as well pre-download it to be ready for April 27/28. On launch day, you’ll also need to download a smaller patch, version 3.0.1.

In case you missed it, we published our Lord of Hatred review earlier in the week. Give it a read if you’re curious about the expansion’s impact on the narrative, and how it changes core Diablo 4 gameplay.

#3949. Guide: GTA 6: Secret Controls the Game Doesn't Tell You

GTA 6 has a complicated control scheme that allows you to interact with the game in a variety of different ways. And while Rockstar does a good job introducing almost all of the title's mechanics, several useful features and commands are never mentioned at all. In this GTA 6 guide, we're going to tell you about some of its secret controls.

On this page: Best Secret Controls GTA 6 Doesn't Tell You

Below are 12 secret controls in GTA 6 the game doesn't tell you about.

Please note, these all apply to the Default control scheme, which you can enable by pressing Options > Settings > Control Scheme.

Double tap Triangle to get out of your car while the engine's still running:

This can be useful for when you need to make a swift getaway, as you want waste time needing to start the engine.

One other quick tip here: if you're with a partner and need to quickly get into the back seat, hold Triangle so your character doesn't waste time running around to the passenger side.

If the police know your identity but not necessarily your car, one way you can avoid being detected is by hiding behind the wheel.

Just park up somewhere discreet, and hold Circle to hide from any pursuing police:

You can rest and lean on any surface by standing close to it and holding the Circle button, like shown:

This can be useful if you're casing a joint, or just want to watch the world pass you by.

You don't always need words to get your point across. There are situations where a middle finger will do.

Fortunately, GTA 6 has a solution for scenarios just like that.

While on foot, hold L2 and press R1 to give someone the finger:

You can also do this while driving by simply pressing R1 while behind the wheel:

Tapping Left and Right while driving will turn on your indicators, allowing you to signal to other motorists which way you're going:

This can actually be useful when you're trying to drive safely, as oncoming cars will understand which way you're going and react accordingly. It can also help when you're merging lanes on motorways.

While more complex radio controls can be accessed by holding Left, did you know you can also quickly turn the radio on and off by double-tapping Left?

This works both in a car and when you're out and about using your earbuds.

If you press Square while driving, you can quickly attack with your car door, as shown:

This is really useful when you're being flanked by unsuspecting bikers — or you just want to show cyclists who's king the road!

Much like the above car door attack, you can kick any nearby enemies by pushing Square while you're riding a bike, as shown:

This can help you knock rival motorcylists off their bike, or just give you a good core workout while on the highway.

You can go first-person at any time while you're on-foot and stationary by holding L2 and pressing R3:

You can move the camera around from this position and press R2 to zoom, but you do need to hold L2 down throughout.

It's also worth noting you can't move while doing this, as there's no traditional first-person mode in the game.

This can be useful for reading signs and other looking closely at other objects in the game, though.

Every vehicle has a full suite of options you can access by holding Left and using the right analogue stick to navigate up to Vehicle, as shown:

These options can include everything from winding down your windows to turning on your headlights. Speaking of which, you can also toggle your headlights at any time by pressing Circle:

And, if you're in a boat, you can use the above vehicle management options to set down an anchor, which will keep it in place while you go diving:

If you're playing on the PS5, the DualSense controller's adaptive triggers will help you observe the speed limit.

While you're driving, holding R2 until you feel the first point of resistance. This is the speed limit.

You'll need to have Adaptive Triggers Resistance enabled to feel this, and you can check it's on by pressing Options > Settings > Controller > DualSense Wireless Controller Features:

You can take two cars when you're with your partner by using the command menu.

Hold Right to bring up the menu and press Cross/X to instruct your partner to drive:

Then get in another car and hold Right again then press Square to follow you:

You'll notice that your partner will drive right behind you, which can be useful if you need to setup getaway cars during robberies:

Did you know about any or all of these secret controls in GTA 6? You can find even more tips and tricks through the link, as well as tons of collectible and mission walkthroughs in our GTA 6 guide.

#3948. Rockstar firings tribunal hears closing statements, with judge promising to deliver a verdict "as quickly as I possibly can" - though it may take a while

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Said judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as quickly as [she] possibly can".

That's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can."

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

To recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a new company Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the big game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".
